public_rationale: Part of the claim has support. Graphite's measurements show that primarily AI-generated articles rose from almost none to 36% of new web articles within a year of ChatGPT, and to 48% by two years. But the claim says this made the information people find worse, and that Altman and Nadella caused it. A later Graphite study found most articles shown in Google Search and in chatbot citations were human-written, which cuts against the quality part. I found no study that ties any decline in the quality of information found to OpenAI and Microsoft in particular. The evidence does not settle the causal claim.
limitations: Detector-based estimates of AI content are approximate.
The search-visibility study falls after the target period.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Sam Altman's and Satya Nadella's push for LLMs has filled the internet with junk and made online information worse.

statement.excerpt: It’s harder now because of Mark Zuckerberg and Sundar Pichai, and the information you look for is worse because of Sam Altman and Satya Nadella, whose deranged attachment to Large Language Models have pumped our internet full of bullshit at a time when Google had actively abandoned any duty to the web or its users.

our_interpretation: Plain reading: LLM products pushed by OpenAI (Altman) and Microsoft (Nadella) led to a flood of low-quality AI-generated content online, and this made the information people find worse.

Testing it needs two things: evidence of a large rise in AI-generated content after ChatGPT, and evidence that this lowered the quality of what people actually find. It also needs a way to attribute that to these two leaders rather than to LLMs in general.
Target period: ChatGPT's launch (November 2022) to the post date.
criteria.support_condition: Studies show a large rise in AI-generated web content since ChatGPT, that this content made search results or information found worse, and that the rise traces mainly to OpenAI and Microsoft tools.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Studies show AI content did not rise much, or that it did not reach users or lower the quality of results, or that it was driven by other actors.

evidence.excerpt: Within the first 12 months, the percentage of primarily AI-generated articles jumped to 36%, and reached 48% by 24 months.
evidence.explanation: Shows a large rise in AI-generated web articles after ChatGPT. This supports the 'pumped our internet full' part, though not the cause or the quality effect.

evidence.excerpt: 86 percent of articles appearing in Google Search and 82 percent of those that appear on ChatGPT and Perplexity were written by people.
evidence.explanation: An October 2025 measurement, after the target period, suggesting that AI content mostly does not reach search users. That cuts against 'the information you look for is worse'.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: A study measuring the quality of search results or information over 2022-2025 that attributes changes to AI-generated content from OpenAI and Microsoft tools.
